newsitem.title: USA: Stocks steady after early ziz-zagging.
newsitem.headline: Stocks steady after early ziz-zagging.

text.p: Stocks stabilised at midsession Thursday after zig-zagging on pressures stemming from a fast-falling dollar and weak bonds.
At 1 p.m. EST, the Dow Jones industrial average was up 4.47 points at 6,182.18, surpassing Wednesday's record closing high of 6,177.71.
In the broader market, declining issues led advances 12-9 on active volume of 278 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index was up 6.22 points at 1,251.71. The American Stock Exchange index was up 0.25 at 578.12.
After storming 97 points higher Wednesday, the Dow rose slightly in early trading, then lost nearly 30 points before rallying back into the plus column.

"We had a 90-plus (Dow) point day yesterday, so for the market to hold on to all of that ... is extraordinary," said Tom Carpenter, chief economist of ASB Capital Management Inc. "The underpinning of the market is very bullish."
The dollar fell sharply after one of Japan's most influential policy-makers, known in financial markets as "Mr. Yen," signalled that the U.S. currency's recovery was about to end.
In New York trading, the dollar sank to 111.43 Japanese yen from 113.95 Wednesday, and it fell to 1.5065 German marks from 1.5175 marks.

Analysts said the dollar's retreat fuelled concerns on Wall Street that the Group of Three -- Japan, Germany and the United States -- had waited until after the U.S. elections to hint that their consensus for a strong dollar was breaking down.
A weak dollar could scare off foreign investors, whose buying has contributed to Wall Street's strength.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year Treasury lost 23/32 and its yield rose to 6.67 percent from 6.62 percent on Wednesday.

Technology stocks were big gainers, aided by Intel Corp.'s forecast of sharply higher sales and profit margins in the fourth quarter due to strong demand for personal computer chips. Intel rose 3-3/8 to 122-1/4.
International Business Machines rose 1/2 to 133-3/4, Cisco added 1-3/8 to 62-5/8, Dell was up 1-1/4 to 88-3/8 and Microsoft gained 1/8 to 144-5/8.
James Cramer, president of Cramer Co., said that despite the rally, technology stocks are still good buys.
"IBM's at a bargain, I bought some of that. And CompUSA." He added, "I like it here. I'm not worried about a post (election) hangover and believe technology looks incredibly good."
But Ken Tower, a technical analyst at UST Securities, noted that "The big tech stocks are doing well, but it has not been a broad-based tech rally."

Among special situations, Lowe's Cos. lost 4-5/8 to 38-7/8 after forecasting that its third-quarter earnings would top Wall Street's expectations but its fourth-quarter results would be disappointing.
